system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2185-03-27 18:37:00 to 2185-04-02 13:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of sclerosing mesenteritis, chronic abdominal pain, and G-tube dependence was readmitted three days after discharge due to worsening nausea, vomiting, and dehydration. She presented with acute kidney injury, metabolic alkalosis, and hypokalemia, all of which resolved with IV hydration and electrolyte repletion. During admission, she developed aspiration pneumonitis after vomiting, prompting a course of levofloxacin, and had ongoing suicidal ideation, requiring intermittent 1:1 sitter monitoring and psychiatric evaluation. Imaging showed paralytic ileus without obstruction, and a midline was placed for IV access due to limited central venous options. She improved clinically, was stabilized on oral medications, and was discharged home with plans for outpatient follow-up, antibiotic completion, and continued social work support for TPN insurance approval.
problems: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus

Brief Hospital Course:
HOSPITAL SUMMARY: Ms. ___ is a ___ with poor gastric 
motility, sclerosing mesenteritis, numerous GI surgeries, s/p 
decompression G-tube placement, who presents with intractable 
nausea/vomiting and resulting dehydration. She received 1L of 
IVF in the ED and another 1L on the wards with subsequent 
improvement in her labs and symptoms.  She had only occasional 
vomiting during this admission (many days with no episodes at 
all) and was able to maintain hydration and stable weight at 
~155 lbs. 

ACTIVE ISSUES:

# NAUSEA/VOMITING: Patient has a longstanding history of nausea 
and vomiting and has a G-tube in place for decompression. She 
has had frequent admissions for dehydration in the past which 
have been responsive to IVF. She has tried to obtain insurance 
approval to receive IVF and/or TPN at home, but so far has been 
unable to do so (per her outpatient gastroenterologist Dr. ___, 
___ needs to fill out insurance paperwork). She initially 
presented with a concern of ~10 lbs of weight loss; however, on 
our inpatient standing scale her weight was 152-155 lbs during 
this admission, which is consistent with her prior weights (she 
reports that her weight on her home scale prior to admission was 
only 143). Also, her albumin of 4.4 suggests that she is 
maintaining decent nutrition despite frequent episodes of 
vomiting at this time.  She received her home nausea regimen 
with occasional additional doses of IV phenergan and IV 
lorazepam, which she felt were more effective for her.  She 
reported persistent nausea throughout this admission, though the 
vomiting was markedly improved after IV fluids. She did not 
receive further IVF after one liter on hospital day #1 and was 
able to maintain hydration. Of note, she was noted by nursing 
staff to eat large portions of very heavy things (bacon, 
omelettes, ___ fries, other fried foods) and there was a 
general perception that her nausea may have been helped by 
smaller, more frequent meals of less fatty foods. This was 
suggested to her during this admission.

# ABDOMINAL PAIN: Patient had her chronic abdominal pain during 
this admission. She received her home morphine for pain control 
plus two additional one-time doses of 1 mg IV dilaudid.  Her 
pain waxed and waned over the course of this admission, but was 
generally controlled to her baseline level.  

# FEAR OF FALLING: Patient reported a feeling of being 
off-balance and ""like I don't know when my feet are hitting the 
floor."" Neurological exam was normal (somewhat slow 
heel-to-shin, but reasonably accurate), including intact 
sensation in feet and intact proprioception. She was seen by 
physical therapy who felt she was safe for discharge home, and 
recommended use of a walker as needed for reassurance/stability 
as well as a home safety evaluation to identify potential 
contributors to fall risk in her home environment.

# SOCIAL ISSUES: The patient continues to have significant 
social stressors and to feel more comfortable being in the 
hospital where she can be observed than at home where she feels 
it is only a matter of time before she becomes dehydrated again 
and feels she lacks social support. During her prior admission, 
there was a lengthy meeting with her inpatient and outpatient 
providers (including case management and social work) with 
resulting recommendation to have frequent and reliable 
outpatient follow up and as much continuity of care as possible 
while admitted. However, unfortunately the hospital is not 
organized in such a way as to ensure continuity of care for 
inpatients, and on this occasion the patient was admitted to a 
new floor with new nurses, under a new attending, and assigned 
to a new social worker. She did not endorse SI (as at her last 
admission), though she does continue to suffer from depression. 
She was continued on her outpatient regimen.

# IV ACCESS: In the past, Ms. ___ has been noted to have 
difficult IV access and she has required a PICC/midline for IVF 
and TPN. During this admission, she was felt to not require TPN, 
and peripheral IVs were placed.

INACTIVE ISSUES:

home medications.

HOSPITAL SUMMARY: Ms. ___ is a ___ with poor gastric 
motility, sclerosing mesenteritis, numerous GI surgeries, s/p 
decompression G-tube placement, who presents with intractable 
nausea/vomiting and resulting dehydration. She received 1L of

improvement in her labs and symptoms.  She had only occasional 
vomiting during this admission (many days with no episodes at 
all) and was able to maintain hydration and stable weight at

ACTIVE ISSUES:

# NAUSEA/VOMITING: Patient has a longstanding history of nausea 
and vomiting and has a G-tube in place for decompression. She 
has had frequent admissions for dehydration in the past which 
have been responsive to IVF. She has tried to obtain insurance 
approval to receive IVF and/or TPN at home, but so far has been 
unable to do so (per her outpatient gastroenterologist Dr. ___, 
___ needs to fill out insurance paperwork). She initially 
presented with a concern of ~10 lbs of weight loss; however, on 
our inpatient standing scale her weight was 152-155 lbs during 
this admission, which is consistent with her prior weights (she 
reports that her weight on her home scale prior to admission was 
only 143). Also, her albumin of 4.4 suggests that she is 
maintaining decent nutrition despite frequent episodes of 
vomiting at this time.  She received her home nausea regimen 
with occasional additional doses of IV phenergan and IV 
lorazepam, which she felt were more effective for her.  She 
reported persistent nausea throughout this admission, though the 
vomiting was markedly improved after IV fluids. She did not 
receive further IVF after one liter on hospital day #1 and was 
able to maintain hydration. Of note, she was noted by nursing 
staff to eat large portions of very heavy things (bacon, 
omelettes, ___ fries, other fried foods) and there was a 
general perception that her nausea may have been helped by 
smaller, more frequent meals of less fatty foods. This was

pain waxed and waned over the course of this admission, but was 
generally controlled to her baseline level.

off-balance and ""like I don't know when my feet are hitting the

as well as a home safety evaluation to identify potential 
contributors to fall risk in her home environment.

social stressors and to feel more comfortable being in the 
hospital where she can be observed than at home where she feels 
it is only a matter of time before she becomes dehydrated again 
and feels she lacks social support. During her prior admission, 
there was a lengthy meeting with her inpatient and outpatient 
providers (including case management and social work) with 
resulting recommendation to have frequent and reliable 
outpatient follow up and as much continuity of care as possible 
while admitted. However, unfortunately the hospital is not 
organized in such a way as to ensure continuity of care for 
inpatients, and on this occasion the patient was admitted to a 
new floor with new nurses, under a new attending, and assigned 
to a new social worker. She did not endorse SI (as at her last 
admission), though she does continue to suffer from depression. 
She was continued on her outpatient regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping take care of you during this stay. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. Honestly, I’m exhausted. I’ve been vomiting nonstop—like a liter or more every day. I feel so weak and dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The team told me you’ve lost about 13 pounds since your last discharge. That’s significant. We’ve started you on IV fluids to help rehydrate you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been trying to keep track in my intake/output diary. It’s been negative for over a week. I just can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We checked your labs, and your kidney function was a bit off when you came in—creatinine was 1.3—but it’s already improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My kidneys were bad last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was mild this time, likely from dehydration. With fluids, it’s already coming back to normal. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’m just so tired of being in and out of the hospital for this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’ve been through a lot. We’re continuing your usual nausea meds—promethazine and octreotide—and added IV Phenergan and lorazepam since you said they work better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the IV ones help more. The oral ones don’t stay down long enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep using IV as needed. Your G-tube is still working well for decompression, so that’s helping too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I wish I could just get IV fluids at home. I wouldn’t have to keep coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Dr. Patel mentioned you’re still working on insurance approval for home IV or TPN. You may need to complete some paperwork to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying, but it’s so frustrating. No one seems to follow through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have social work check in with you. They might be able to help coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look much better—creatinine is down to 0.9, and your electrolytes are stabilizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I only threw up once last night. I think the fluids are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your weight is stable at 155 pounds. That’s a good sign you’re not losing more fluid than you’re taking in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried I’d lost more. My home scale said 143, but I guess it’s not accurate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hospital scales are more reliable. And your albumin is 4.4, which means your nutrition is holding up despite the vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve been eating when I can—bacon, eggs, fries. I know it’s not healthy, but it’s what I can keep down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard the nurses mention that. Fatty foods might actually make nausea worse for some people. Have you tried smaller, lighter meals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I get so hungry when I’m not vomiting, I just eat whatever I want.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I get that. But maybe we could try something like toast, crackers, or broth between meals. It might help reduce nausea long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can try. But I don’t want to feel hungrier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with nutrition to suggest some options. Small, frequent meals might help balance that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today? Still around your abdomen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s constant. It’s not sharp, but it’s there. My usual morphine helps, but sometimes I need more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you two doses of IV Dilaudid, and you said it helped. We’ll keep using your home pain plan unless it’s not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. I just hate feeling like this all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Chronic pain is tough. We’ll keep supporting you with meds and comfort measures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed you’ve been saying you feel off-balance. Like your feet aren’t hitting the floor right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. It’s scary. I’m afraid I’ll fall, especially at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your neuro exam was normal—sensation, strength, coordination are all intact. But physical therapy saw you and thinks a walker could help with stability.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A walker? I don’t want to seem frail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not about frailty—it’s about safety. You’ll have a visiting nurse come to your home to check for fall risks too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, if it helps me stay safe. I do feel better knowing someone will check the house.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve gone two full days without vomiting. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel nauseous, but I’m keeping fluids down. I even ate some soup yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. We’re stopping IV fluids now since you’re maintaining hydration on your own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a day or two. We want to make sure you’re stable and have support at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. Last time, I got dehydrated again within days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. That’s why we’re setting up the visiting nurse and encouraging you to follow up with Dr. Patel. We want to catch things early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ECG showed some changes—slower heart rate, more left axis deviation—but it’s stable compared to before. Nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart’s always been fast. It’s usually in the 120s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and now it’s down to 78. That’s probably because you’re better hydrated. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I do feel less shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. You’ll go home with your usual meds and the visiting nurse visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad to be going home, but I’ll miss having help nearby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re stronger now, and we’re setting up support. Call your husband or PCP if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll try those smaller meals. Maybe it’ll help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of sclerosing mesenteritis, chronic nausea, and G-tube dependence was admitted for intractable vomiting and dehydration. She had lost weight and had a negative fluid balance for over a week. IV fluids were given, leading to improvement in kidney function and stabilization of weight at approximately 155 pounds. Nausea persisted but vomiting decreased significantly, and she was able to maintain hydration without further IV support. Pain was managed with her home morphine and occasional IV Dilaudid. She reported a sensation of imbalance, prompting a physical therapy evaluation and recommendation for a walker and home safety assessment. Social concerns about lack of support and difficulty obtaining home IV therapy were noted. She was discharged home with visiting nurse services, continued medications, and follow-up plans.
